name: West German fat lava
summary: Vases and bowls from West German factories between 1960 and 1980. A thick, bubbled and cratered glaze runs over a moulded earthenware body, in orange, brown, green or yellow.

philosophy.core_thesis: A thick glaze that is allowed to run, bubble and crater gives a mass-made vase the look of cooled volcanic rock.
design_principles: Mould the earthenware body in a bold, round or flared shape with a wide opening.
Apply the lava glaze in a layer of 1 to 3 mm, and add a second thinner glaze over it.
Let the glaze run and crater, so that no two vases are the same.
Choose a bright ground: orange, yellow, green or brown, with a white or black drip.
Make large floor vases of 40 to 60 cm and table vases of 15 to 30 cm.
Add a relief of rings, bands or bubbles in the mould, to give the glaze a place to pool.
Fire at 1000 to 1100 °C in a tunnel kiln.
Mark the base with the factory name, a model number and a height in cm.
anti_patterns: A painted flower or a printed pattern

form.shape: Floor vases, bottle vases, wide bowls, planters and baluster vases with a bold, round or flared outline.
form.profile: A heavy, swelling belly, a wide flared mouth or a bulb on a short neck; relief rings or wave bands often run round the form.
form.foot_and_rim: A wide, flat base with a stamped mark; the rim is thick and rounded and may be wavy.
form.proportion: Height 15 to 60 cm; the wall is 6 to 12 mm and the weight is high for the size.
rules: Mould the form with a thick wall to carry a heavy glaze.
Keep the base flat and stamped.
Place the lava glaze on the upper two thirds and keep the base plain.

bodies.rule: Use a red or white earthenware that is cast or pressed in a mould. A thick body keeps the glaze from warping the piece.

methods: spraying and dipping of the glaze
hand application of the second glaze
forming.joins: A vase is cast in two halves and joined; the seam is fettled and hidden under the glaze.
forming.details: A stamped factory mark, a model number and a glaze that is thick, crusted and uneven.

glaze.pattern: A thick, bubbled and cratered lava glaze in orange, brown or green, with a drip of a second colour over the shoulder.
glaze.gloss: Satin to gloss in the thin parts, matt in the crater; about 10 to 60 GU.
glaze.wear: The crust of the lava glaze is hard but can chip at the rim, and the body may show through at the edge.

palette.strategy: Strong, warm colours of the 1960s and 1970s: orange, brown, mustard and green, with a cream or black drip.

firing.kiln: A gas or electric tunnel kiln, with a biscuit firing and a glaze firing.
processes: slip casting and fettling of the body
spraying of the lava glaze, in a layer of 1 to 3 mm
firing.scale: Thousands of vases each year from each factory; every vase has its own glaze pattern.
firing.signs: A stamped mark, a thick glaze, craters, bubbles, and drips on the shoulder.

emotion.target_response: A feeling of bold fun and warm nostalgia: the viewer sees a thick, bubbled colour and thinks of a 1970s living room.

use_cases: a 1970s interior prompt with a bold vase
a museum label on West German ceramics
avoid_when: the brief needs a refined form
the brief needs a calm, pale palette
the brief needs hand-thrown irregular clay

modifiers.how: Use a thin stoneware or porcelain wall, a single matt glaze and a precise profile.
Replace the lava glaze with flat bright glaze and bold printed stripes or dots.
